title: Jesse Plemons on inheriting Plutarch from Philip Seymour Hoffman
body_md:
In an interview published on November 26, 2026, Jesse Plemons discussed taking on the role of Plutarch Heavensbee in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping. The actor described the opportunity to portray a character previously played by Philip Seymour Hoffman as an honor, while acknowledging that his feelings about inheriting the role are complicated.

Plutarch was introduced to film audiences in Catching Fire as an influential figure within the Capitol. His apparent loyalty to the establishment concealed his support for the resistance. The new prequel takes place approximately twenty-five years earlier, giving Plemons an opportunity to explore a younger version of the character before the relationships and commitments seen in the original films had fully developed.

Plemons has a personal connection to Hoffman's work beyond the Hunger Games franchise. Hoffman played his father in Paul Thomas Anderson's The Master, and Plemons considers him one of his favorite actors. Nevertheless, the younger Plutarch was not conceived as a direct imitation of Hoffman's performance. The substantial chronological gap allows for a different energy, greater ambition and relationships that are only beginning to take shape.

Director Francis Lawrence worked with producer Nina Jacobson and author Suzanne Collins to develop Plutarch's story. Their adaptation includes scenes that were not present in the novel, intended to clarify his difficult position within the Capitol. One important addition involves an encounter with President Snow, played by Ralph Fiennes. Plutarch must maintain the appearance of loyalty while protecting the resistance from discovery.

Plemons and Lawrence also discussed whether Plutarch's actions might be motivated partly by personal ambition, resentment toward the Capitol or a desire to become a hero. Plemons ultimately favored an interpretation in which the character's moral commitment is genuine despite his privileged background. He questioned whether someone motivated entirely by self-interest would sustain such a difficult commitment over decades.

That interpretation does not make Plutarch uncomplicated. Plemons remained interested in how far the character might be willing to sacrifice other people for a larger objective, particularly in his developing relationship with Haymitch. The tension between affection, pragmatism and political commitment gives the performance much of its complexity.

The actor also expressed interest in seeing a story about Plutarch's teenage years, although he acknowledged that he would not be suited to playing that age himself. His suggestion is a personal creative preference, not confirmation of another production. The interview offers insight into how the prequel uses a familiar character to explore realistic hope, moral ambiguity and the costs of resistance.
